## TL;DR

Completed the remote-validation hang recovery work and addressed the latest review findings. A failed or slow load probe remains unknown and cannot independently trigger a kill. A positive runner-side container CPU sample protects a progressing container even when the laptop has stopped receiving output. Before a hang kill removes a container, the runner captures recent Docker logs and inspect state and attaches them to the task event; the Debug panel shows that evidence when expanded. Container reaping now runs on probed hosts, logs each removal, and checks the inspected name prefix before removing old validation containers. The scoped check passed after I fixed a formatter issue and a failing changed-test fixture.

## Work and rationale

I began by reading the current task specification and the latest review report. The review called out three concrete gaps: whether reaping was actually scheduled, whether captured evidence was visible to users, and whether Docker substring filters could select unrelated names. The current source already contained the primary implementation for conservative hang detection and evidence capture. I traced each path rather than duplicating it: unknown load has no idle conclusion, explicit host-side CPU activity prevents a kill, the finalizer captures before issuing removal, and the Debug panel projects the structured evidence into expanded event details.

The scheduling path uses `containerReaperDue(undefined, now)` to make a host eligible for its first sweep. The host loop stores the current time only after confirming the sweep is due, then sends the reaper command asynchronously. I added a behavioral host-pool test that probes a host, calls the scheduler again after it becomes available, verifies the reaper command was sent, and checks that output from the reaper reaches the system logger. This covers scheduling and visibility rather than only checking the command string.

Both the periodic reaper and stopped-container cleanup use a prefix-restricted candidate filter and then inspect each container name before removal. The explicit shell prefix check is the safety boundary because Docker’s name filters can match substrings. The reaper uses the 25-minute run cap, checks the creation time, and emits a readable line for each removal. The hang event carries the condition that fired plus the bounded log and inspect excerpts. The UI type and Debug panel render these fields, and the existing focused tests cover capture order and evidence display.

The failure-classification path records a stable human-readable cause for degraded hosts instead of copying arbitrary test output into the host-status reason. This keeps convincing text printed by tests from being mistaken for a real runner fault. Hang messages likewise identify the observed condition in plain language.

## Approaches tried

The first required changed-path check ran remotely and built successfully, but surfaced two test failures: the new scheduler test was not simulating streamed command output, and the existing changed-test selector fixture could not load the external Vite config from its synthetic Git repository. I changed the mock transport to invoke its output callback, matching the real transport, and confirmed the scheduler test passed alone.

For the selector test, I inspected the full Rolldown error. It showed that its config entry path was resolved from the synthetic repository root and could not be found when the config lived outside that root. Placing the fixture under the system temporary directory and then symlinking the config did not fix resolution. I instead gave the fixture a small local Vitest config that discovers the checkout’s test files from a relative path while keeping its Git refs rooted in the synthetic repository. The targeted selector test then passed.

The next scoped check passed the remote build and changed tests, rendered contrast, and UI smoke, but the local format check found a formatting issue in the new scheduler test. I ran `bun run fmt` as directed and reran the required check. That run passed on thinkpad and locally, including the changed-path tests, formatting, lint, build, static guards, both contrast audits, and UI smoke.

## Challenges and blockers

The remote gate takes several minutes because it provisions dependencies, builds, and runs the selected regression suite on the runner. Its link probe and transfer completed, and the remote gate passed. An initial test failure was a genuine mock setup defect; the other was an existing fixture-resolution issue exposed by the required changed-path suite. Both were corrected and verified before the final check. The first local pass also required a formatter run and another full check. The final check completed without a failing step.

No live production hang or leaked runner container was available for a real-device recovery trial during this session. The behavior is covered through deterministic tests and the remote gate; this report makes no claim that a real leaked container was observed or reaped here.

## Key learnings

The laptop’s output stream and load probe are incomplete evidence about a remote run. Treating failed probes as unknown and asking the host about the container avoids equating a broken SSH stream with an idle process. Capturing logs and inspect state before removal preserves evidence that would otherwise disappear with the container. Docker name filters need an explicit inspected-prefix guard before cleanup. Finally, a useful test of periodic maintenance must exercise the scheduler and its logging path, not just inspect generated shell text.
